justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assumed was a recent price level near $365–366 for the underlying asset (likely SPY or a similar broad equity index ETF). At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price with only a small positive drift, reflecting the general long-run upward bias in equity markets but essentially treating the next session as close to a random walk around the current level. At the one-week horizon, I allowed for slightly more drift, consistent with a weekly expected return in the range of 0.3–0.5%. At the one-month horizon, the point estimate of $372 implies roughly a 1.5–2% gain, which is broadly consistent with historical average monthly equity returns. None of these estimates embed any strong directional view; they are primarily driven by the historical tendency of equity indices to drift upward over time.

The confidence interval widths reflect realized volatility assumptions appropriate to each horizon. For the one-day interval, I used an implied daily volatility consistent with an annualized figure somewhere in the 15–20% range, which produces a roughly ±$9–10 range at the 90% level. As the horizon extends to one week and one month, uncertainty compounds with the square root of time, which is why the one-month interval ($338–$406) is substantially wider than the one-day interval. The intervals also implicitly account for the fact that intraday and day-to-day returns are not perfectly normal — fat tails in equity returns mean extreme moves are somewhat more likely than a pure Gaussian model would suggest, which I tried to partially accommodate by widening the tails modestly.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden macro shock — such as an unexpected Federal Reserve policy announcement, a geopolitical escalation, a credit event, or a significant deterioration in economic data — could produce a move of 5–10% or more within even a single week, which would breach the lower bound of my one-week and possibly one-month intervals. On the upside, a strongly positive catalyst such as a surprise rate cut, a major geopolitical resolution, or a blowout earnings season could push prices above the upper bounds. Liquidity crises or flash crash dynamics represent tail risks that are particularly hard to quantify but could temporarily push prices far outside any reasonable interval before a recovery.

Finally, it is worth noting that my intervals are unconditional — they do not condition on any specific known upcoming events. If there is a scheduled FOMC meeting, major economic data release, or earnings report from a heavily weighted index constituent within the forecast horizon, the true uncertainty is likely higher than my stated intervals suggest.
